scenarios.title: Let an operator mount their own archive
scenarios.summary: Repair an ordinary caller’s mount permission and prove who can end the session.
scenarios.objective: Let either ordinary operator start a read-only session on /media/archive, without an automatic startup request. Among ordinary operators, only the actual mounter may unmount it; an already-mounted request must not transfer that authority. The administrator remains allowed to unmount. Finish with /media/archive mounted by Alex, with noexec, nosuid and nodev set in the applied options. Preserve the required /srv/data saved entry and actual administrator mount; leave /media/personal unmounted and keep its supplied entry. Keep all supplied mountpoints and stable UUID identities. The same policy must handle the supplied callers, missing media and changed device aliases.
scenarios.retry_guidance: Read the first unmet requirement. Compare the saved entry with the actual mounter and applied flags; then retry with the appropriate caller.
steps: Save policy and perform the required session actions
Check both the current session and supplied cases

guide.title: Understand the mount permission boundary
guide.why: user permits any ordinary operator to mount the configured entry. Among ordinary operators, only its actual mounter can unmount it. It is not a setting that names Alex or another account. With neither user nor users, mounting requires the administrator. An already-mounted request does not become a new mount or change its mounter.
guide.action: Review the supplied media and callers.

guide.title: Save policy and perform the required session actions
guide.why: The fourth field of each six-field entry contains comma-separated options. ro selects read-only mounting and noauto keeps the entry out of this table’s startup requests. user and users also imply noexec, nosuid and nodev. A later exec, suid or dev can undo the corresponding restriction. We inspect these policy flags; this simulator does not execute files, set-user-ID programs or device nodes.
guide.action: Edit the simulated table, Save configuration, then use Mount or Unmount.

guide.title: Check both the current session and supplied cases
guide.why: Save configuration updates the simulated table. It does not remount a filesystem, replace its actual mounter or rewrite already-applied flags. Inspect Current mounts, then use the proper caller to unmount and mount again when a task requires changed live options. Current saved policy controls ordinary unmount authorization.
guide.action: Choose Check work and inspect the first unmet requirement.

scenarios.explanation: The user option permits ordinary mounting without giving every operator unmount authority. noauto keeps startup from requesting the archive, ro selects read-only mode, and the three implied restrictions are recorded when mounting. The real successful mounter is retained; a repeated mount request is not a handover.
hints: Compare user and users with the requested ordinary unmount boundary.
Look for a later option that overrides an implied restriction; saved and applied flags can differ.
Use the appropriate caller to end the old session, then mount using the requested final caller.
scenarios.simplifications: Source check2026-11-04: LPIC-1 v5.0 objective104.3 (partial), mount/fstab/umount manuals and versioned util-linux v2.41 permission rules. Fixed supplied ext4/xfs media, mountpoints and three simulated callers; no host mount or UID lookup. Supported options are defaults, ro/rw, auto/noauto, nofail, one user/users/nouser token and exec/noexec, suid/nosuid, dev/nodev in order. The supplied base permits those three flags; defaults is a no-op here, not a universal kernel default. Mixed/repeated permission tokens, owner/group, user=NAME, helpers, command-line option merging, filesystem access/ACLs, busy/lazy/forced unmount, hot removal, nested/network mounts, polkit and namespaces are outside this slice. Flags are audited policy properties, not demonstrated execution effects. Each supplied target supports one mount. An identical repeated request is a no-op here; real Linux stacked mounts are not simulated.

scenarios.title: Hand over shared media without widening personal access
scenarios.summary: Repair a shared handover, apply corrected options, and preserve a personal sibling’s boundary.
scenarios.objective: Enable a shared handover of /media/archive: either ordinary operator must be able to unmount it. Keep /media/personal limited to its actual mounter among ordinary operators. Finish with /media/archive mounted read-only by Casey, with noexec, nosuid and nodev set in the applied options; saving text alone must not alter an existing mount. Preserve the required /srv/data saved entry and actual administrator mount, and keep /media/personal mounted by Alex with its supplied restrictions. Keep all supplied mountpoints and stable UUID identities. The same policy must handle the supplied caller, missing-media and changed-alias cases.

guide.title: Understand the mount permission boundary
guide.why: user permits any ordinary operator to mount, but only that actual mounter may unmount it. users permits ordinary operators to unmount each other’s mounts. Neither option names a particular account. Here the shared entry needs users, while the personal sibling keeps user; administrator actions remain available.
guide.action: Review the supplied media and callers.

scenarios.explanation: Changing user to users permits the second ordinary caller to detach the shared mount, while the personal entry remains mounter-only. Fixing a later exec override repairs the saved policy, but the old applied flag persists until unmount/remount. Preserve the administrator data mount and the sibling’s actual mounter.
